doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: The jam session where a waltz exposed him: lesson from Donald Bailey
summary: At an early jam session he played four-four against a three-four tune, and Donald Bailey explained odd measures to him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: You also said that you learn under pressure. Give us if you can a situation in which you learned to do something under pressure.

Well when I first started to play man, before I played my first gig I would practice and practice because I didn’t go to, I couldn’t afford to go to school, so I learned from friends you know, and we’d play. And I went to this jam session one time, and I mean you’re talking about embarrassing, man, but it really made me go to work. I mean I learned a very valuable lesson that night. It was time for me to play. Everybody had a time to play you know? So they started to play [scats] Waltzhatten. It’s a three-four rhythm. And I say
Uh oh, uh oh, talk about polyrhythms.

But I didn’t know nothing about no polyrhythms back then you know. ‘Cause I was self taught you know, and I had never heard a waltz before you know. I mean not to know that it was a waltz. So anyway, the guys are turning around and looking at me man, and I’m wondering what’s wrong. Because the beat ain’t right, man, it ain’t matching up. So man that’s when I learned that there was a different rhythm other than four-four. But if I hadn’t gone to that jam session and put myself in a position like that, I never would have learned that. I mean it would have taken me even more time. But because I went and had enough nerve to get on stage. So anyway, who pulled my coat -- there’s a great drummer named Donald Bailey. They called him Donald Duck. He used to play drums with Jimmy Smith. Great drummer man. He played with a lot of people. So he got me on the side and he said “Man you know in rhythm, some bars, some measures have four beats, some measures have two beats, some measures have five beats, and some measures have three beats. Some measures even have seven beats.” And then that’s when I learned about the differences you know? And so that was a great lesson for me you know. But you’re talking about pressure man, I started sweating man. But it was beautiful man, because I went and I practiced. And I practiced. And the next time I went to a jam session they didn’t play anything in three-four.
